newsitem.title: RWANDA: Two more sentenced to death in Rwanda for genocide.
newsitem.headline: Two more sentenced to death in Rwanda for genocide.

text.p: A special court in Rwanda has sentenced two more men to death for genocide, bringing the number of capital sentences so far to at least eight.
State radio said on Wednesday Calixte Ngendahimana and Janvier Bavugayubusa were sentenced by a court in Gisenyi on Tuesday. They have 15 days to file an appeal.
Rwanda began a series of trials late last month against the first of 90,000 detainees, overwhelmingly from the majority Hutu tribe, accused of involvement in the 1994 genocide.
Paul Atita, a defence lawyer from Benin, West Africa, brought to Rwanda by a group called Lawyers Without Borders, told Reuters he believed eight defendants had been sentenced to death so far.
Ngendahimana and Bavugayubusa were tried on January 15 when they pleaded guilty to genocide and crimes against humanity, state radio reported at the time.
The reading of the verdict was deferred until January 21.

On Wednesday the radio said Ngendahimana was a member of the "extremist" political party, the Coalition for the Defence of the Republic, and Bavugayubusa was a local leader in the Rwerere commune of Gisenyi prefecture and member of the former ruling party, the National Revolutionary Movement for Development.
About 800,000 minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus are thought to have been slaughtered in the genocide.
Few of the accused have been represented by defence lawyers. Rwanda's 1996 Genocide Law says the government will not pay for a defence but the accused may defend themselves.
Unlike the U.N. tribunal trying some alleged leaders of the genocide in Arusha, Tanzania, the Rwandan courts may impose the death penalty on those convicted of the most serious category of crimes.
The justice ministry says execution will be by firing squad but the government has yet to announce whether the killings will be in public.
